title: Rounded Chart Estimator
context: Grade 5, the page of other units in everyday use. An adult sees a conversion chart. What the page is doing is meeting units used elsewhere, and the one thing a child must carry away is that every answer made from a rounded chart is about, not exact.

writeup.why: Know what each other unit measures, compare it with a metric unit using the chart, estimate a measure by adding a chart number a few times, and say about with every answer.
writeup.look: Seven chart cards along the top, three bins, pairs of bars laid side by side, stacks of one card, and an About stamp.
writeup.stage: Three bands across 1600 by 900. The header runs 0 to 80 and is one line only: 'Rounded Chart Estimator' in ink at the far left, a small dot set clear of the name, the phase title beside the dot on the same line, the host's navigation, and sound and restart as three round controls at the far right. The canvas runs 92 to 746, one rounded card on the paper colour. At its top left, at x 64, y 108 and 330 by 76, sits the running count: the number of copies of a card stacked. It is never a score. The working area is 1086 by 528 at x 64, y 202. The chart lies along the top of the area at y 220 as seven cards, each 140 by 90, from x 90 to x 1070. Each card names one of the other units and gives its rounded metric number with the word about, and the metric side of each card is violet, labelled Unit fact. On the first phase three bins stand along y 560, at x 160, x 480 and x 800, each 240 wide, labelled length, weight and capacity. On the second phase two bar rails run along y 400 and y 470 from x 120, and a tapped card lays its two bars on them roughly to scale, the card's own unit above and the metric unit below. On the third phase the Stack button stands at x 900, y 330, and each tap lays one more copy of the card's bar end to end along y 400, with the metric numbers of the copies listed under the bars for adding. On the fourth phase the About stamp sits at x 900, y 560 and must be pressed onto an answer before it is taken. The measure a question gives is deep blue, labelled Given, the card in use is amber, and the answer turns green, labelled Answer, once it is stamped. Down the right of the canvas, in the same rectangle on every phase and never animated in or out, the question sits above the answer slot at x 1186, y 250 (356 by 92) that holds what the child has given, and under it the pad at x 1170, y 368 (388 by 363). The pad is ten number keys with a point key, a delete key, and a key for each metric unit on the chart. The footer runs 758 to 900: the voice caption at the far left with its speaking dot beside it, measuring its own wrap and dropping a type size rather than spilling, and the phase bar at the right with the question count under it. There is no sidebar and no score box anywhere, and nothing is ever written over the working area. Content colours are the chapter's own, and the nine tools of this chapter share them. The measure the question gives, in the unit it is given in, is deep blue, labelled Given or Measure. The measure the working reaches, and a reading on a scale, is green, labelled Answer, Reading or Same measure. The places moved across the unit chart, and the worth of one small mark on a scale, are vermilion, labelled Move or One mark. A unit fact, the unit names on the chart and the other temperature scale are violet, labelled Unit fact, Unit or Other scale. The part taken away, and a part left over after sharing, are rose, labelled Taken away or Left over. The unit, column, mark or step being worked on now is amber. Grey is kept for a zero holding a place open inside a number, labelled Place holder, and for nothing else. Rulers, tapes, jugs, scales, thermometer tubes, chart lines, arrows, operation signs and step labels are near-black ink, and anything dimmed fades to half strength. Chrome never borrows one of the content colours, and each reading survives with the colour taken away, because a part is told by its written label before it is told by its colour.
writeup.finish: The last stack stays on the stage with its sum beside it, stamped About, in green.

writeup.delight: On the fourth phase the About stamp lands with a soft thump, leaves a round inked mark on the answer, and the answer turns green under it.
writeup.opening: Every mount comes up already furnished for its phase with nothing yet sorted or stacked. On the first phase seven unit cards lie above three bins labelled length, weight and capacity. On the second the chart cards lie along the top with two empty bar rails below. On the third one chart card lies beside the Stack button with a question about a few of that unit. On the fourth an estimate waits in the answer slot with the About stamp beside it. One thing moves, once: the first unit card, the first chart card, the Stack button or the About stamp gives one slow pulse while the voice speaks its opening line.
writeup.freePlay: Any chart card tapped, stacked any number of times and added, with every estimate stamped about. Nothing to get right, no target and no timer. The child is left with the same stage and every control unlocked.

serves.exercise: writing the length of a cricket pitch in metres from yards
writing the weight of a cake in kilograms from pounds
writing an amount of water in litres from gallons
writing the weight of a bag of wheat in pounds from kilograms
writing a distance between two cities in miles from kilometres
writing a weight of cheese in ounces from grams
writing a height in metres and centimetres from feet and inches

source_tool.description: The chart of other units lies along the top of the working area as seven cards. The chart cards read: 1 mile, about 1.61 km; 1 yard, about 0.914 m; 1 foot, about 0.305 m; 1 inch, about 2.54 cm; 1 gallon, about 3.79 L; 1 kg, about 2.2 pounds; 1 ounce, about 28.35 g. The metric side of each card is violet, labelled Unit fact. On the first phase unit cards are dragged into three bins, length, weight and capacity. On the second a card is tapped to lay its two bars side by side, the other unit and the metric unit, drawn roughly to scale. On the third a Stack button lays copies of one chart card end to end, the running count at the top left of the canvas counts the copies, and the child adds their metric numbers. On the fourth an About stamp must be pressed onto an answer before it is taken, and the answer turns green, labelled Answer. The measure a question gives is deep blue, labelled Given, and the card in use is amber.
source_tool.art_direction: Old measuring cups in a kitchen drawer / Picture book

style.text: Least text. One header line, short labels, nothing else. The voice carries the teaching and the caption carries the voice.

stage.note: Every coordinate is authored in 1600x900, so a smartboard and a phone in landscape get one composition. Nothing scrolls. The three bands below are the settled layout, taken from Two Hundred Trail in Class 3 chapter 3 once it was finished; a tool that has to depart from one of them says in its own writeup.stage which band it changed and why.

bands.canvas: 92 to 746. One rounded panel holding everything the child works on.
bands.footer: 758 to 900. The voice at the far left, the phase bar at the right.
bands.header: 0 to 80. One line, and only one.

zones.bar: the phase bar at the right of the footer, the question count under it
zones.pad: under the slot, and furniture on every phase: twelve keys three across where a number is asked for, a word pad where a name or a rule is
zones.name: the tool name at the far left of the header, a measured dot set clear of it
zones.runs: the running count, on the canvas at its top left, never up in the chrome. It counts the thing the tool is actually building; where a tool has nothing to count that corner carries the record being kept instead, and that tool's own stage says so
zones.slot: the question and the child's answer, fixed down the right of the canvas
zones.work: the working area, one thousand and eighty-six by five hundred and twenty-eight
zones.title: the phase title beside that dot, on the same single header line

zones.chrome: again, sound and restart, as round controls at the far right of the header

stage.furniture: The working area is furnished from the first frame. What waits for the child is the count, not the picture: the panels, the slot and the pad are all up and empty before anything is asked.
stage.noSidebar: There is no sidebar. The canvas takes every unit the chrome can spare, because the working area is the tool.
stage.noScoreBox: There is no score box anywhere on the stage. The score leaves on the finished event and it is the host that decides whether to show it, so a child working is never watching a number that judges them.

style.motion: Animate only what carries meaning. Anything that is not changing does not move. Every reward is the maths itself moving, never confetti. Honour prefers-reduced-motion.
drawing: Hand-built inline SVG. No assets and no network, so a school cart works offline.
Chunky rounded forms and large touch targets. A finger is the pointer, not a mouse.

Drawn things, not abstract boxes: a unit chart of seven columns from kilo to milli with the base unit in the middle, rulers and tapes marked in their units, kitchen scales, measuring jugs marked in millilitres, and thermometers with labelled marks.
Every measure is written with its unit on every line, and every decimal names the unit it is in, so 3.04 L is never shown as a bare 3.04.
Every mixed measure shown is ordinary: its smaller part is less than one of the larger unit.
Places are counted from the unit the child has to the unit the child wants, one hop at a time, and each hop shows the number, not the unit, divided or multiplied by 10.
Multiplying and dividing a measure happen in its smallest unit, in whole numbers, and a sharing that does not come out even shows what is left over.
A thermometer shows what one small mark is worth before its column is read, and a Celsius reading sits beside a Fahrenheit one only in the four pairs the chapter prints.
Nothing is animated except the one thing being explained: a hop across the chart, a carry across units, a length shared into equal pieces, or a column rising to a mark.
style.palette_rule: A chrome colour never fills a number, a unit or a mark the child is reading, and a content colour is never used for chrome. This chapter colours the roles a measure plays in a piece of working: the measure the question gives is deep blue, and the measure the working reaches, with a reading taken off a scale, is green; those two are the same two in every tool and every picture of this chapter. The places moved across the unit chart, each one dividing or multiplying the number by 10, and the worth of one small mark on a scale are vermilion. A unit fact such as 1 kg = 1000 g, the unit names on the chart and the other temperature scale are violet. The part taken away, and a remainder left over after sharing, are rose. The unit, column, mark or step being worked on now is amber. A zero holding a place open inside a number is grey. Each role is named in writing first, with the words Given, Answer, Move, Unit fact, Taken away, Left over and Place holder, so the stage still reads with the colour taken away.

rules: Every spoken line is also printed in the caption line at the far left of the footer, so a muted tablet and a child who cannot hear lose nothing.
The caption stays in the footer. Nothing is ever written over the working area.

Numbers are written as words in every line and never as digits, so the voice says four steps and not 4 steps. Handed a digit, a synthesiser reads it in whatever register it likes and the chapter loses the words it is teaching.
The voice never gives the answer. It asks the same question a different way.
It speaks on opening, once when a phase begins, on a miss, and at the finish. It is silent otherwise; a tool that chatters gets muted, and then the first rule is all that is left.
props.muted is honoured at the source, and turning sound off cancels any line already speaking.
voice.where: The caption line sits at the far left of the footer with a small dot beside it that glows while the voice is talking. An again control repeats the last line.
voice.figure: None. The voice speaks with nothing on the stage.
voice.onMiss: Look at the two bars side by side. Which is longer?
voice.onNext: A new card. Read it with the word about.
voice.opening: Seven cards, from a chart of other units.
voice.onFinish: You used the chart's rounded numbers, and said about every time.
voice.onFreePlay: Free play. Tap any card and stack it as often as you like.
voice.figure_rule: A figure appears only where the printed chapter puts one and it has work to do. Everywhere else the voice speaks from the caption line with nothing on the stage: a mascot with no job is one more thing competing with the quantities the child is looking at.
voice.voicePreference: an English voice, female where one is offered

placement.where: After the class has measured small things with a ruler marked in inches on one edge and centimetres on the other. The tool is what lays the unknown units against the known ones and stacks a chart card to build an estimate.

answer_key.rule: Miles, yards, feet and inches measure length; pounds and ounces measure weight; gallons measure capacity. The chart links each to a metric unit with a rounded number: a mile is about 1.61 km, and a kilogram is about 2.2 pounds. For a few lots of a unit, add the chart number that many times. Every answer made from the chart is about, not exact, because the chart's numbers are rounded.
answer_key.wrong: The stage keeps the child's answer and lays its bar beside the stacked cards, so the two lengths are seen apart. An answer without the About stamp waits in the slot with the stamp lit amber beside it. Nothing is cleared and nothing is marked.

hostProps.muted: Sound off. Honour it at the source, not by muting an element later. The captions carry on.
hostProps.phase: number, 1-based, which phase to build. The host chooses the activity; the component builds that phase and nothing else and never moves on by itself.
hostProps.device: tablet / web / smartboard. The stage is a fixed 1600x900 that scales; lay nothing out per device.
hostProps.audience: classroom or solo, and ACCEPTED AND NOT ACTED ON. The teach run and the hint ladder run either way. Kept so the contract is one shape across the book, and named here so nobody reads the shape as a promise.
hostProps.learnQuestions: The four worked items, one per phase, supplied by the host.
hostProps.practiceQuestions: The eight practice items, supplied by the host.

phase_mount.run: A phase is a complete activity in itself and it runs once. The teaching and the doing are not two screens and not two modes: the stage is furnished once, the voice talks over it, and the child starts working on the same stage without anything being rebuilt. Whatever the tool as a whole has to say goes into the FIRST phase's teach run, because there is no opening screen to say it on.
phase_mount.idle: NO AUTO-ADVANCE. After firing, the tool goes idle on the settled phase with the child's work still on it, and stops. Where the host supplies onNext it is drawn and it calls the host back; nothing in the component advances a phase.
phase_mount.prop: phase: number, 1-based, matching writeup.phases[].n. Rounded, clamped, and defaulting to 1 when the host sends nothing, so a bare mount is still a working tool rather than a blank screen. Read once: changing which phase a mount shows is a re-mount.
phase_mount.rule: ONE PHASE, ONE MOUNT. The host says which phase to build by passing `phase`, and the component builds that phase and nothing else. It does not know what came before it and it never moves on by itself.
phase_mount.opening: There is no opening panel and no Start button. The host has already chosen the activity, and a cover screen in front of it is a click between a child and the work. writeup.opening is the first frame of every mount rather than a panel of its own.
phase_mount.completion: The terminal event `finished`, with the phase in its detail, fired exactly once and guarded by a one-shot ref that only a restart re-arms, with the chime and the settle OUTSIDE the guard. props.onComplete is called alongside it: the event is the platform's signal and the callback is the host wrapper's, and firing only one of them leaves a child on a tool that never completes.
phase_mount.notInAMount: No finish card and no free play. Both are the host's now, built out of what the events told it. writeup.finish and writeup.freePlay stay as the record of what they are.

shared_state.note: What getState() returns. These names are a contract: the host reads them to persist and resume a child mid-activity, so renaming one breaks resume. `mode` is gone from this list because there is no mode. `phase` is the phase the host mounted, so a resume restores the work inside a phase and the host restores which phase.

agent_control.reason: Every tool in this chapter is child-operated. There is no agent-driven Concept mode, no postMessage command channel and no narration the tool waits on; the adult, where there is one, talks over the tool rather than through it.

steps: Miles, yards, feet and inches measure length.
So miles and inches are the units of length here.
items.question: Which of these measure length: miles, pounds, inches and gallons?
items.checkpoint: Miles, yards, feet and inches measure length; pounds and ounces measure weight; gallons measure capacity.
items.misconception: Thinking every unit on the chart measures length, when the chart mixes units of length, weight and capacity.

steps: Read the chart card: 1 gallon is about 3.79 L.
About 3.79 L is more than 1 L, so a gallon holds more than a litre.
It is a little less than 4 L.
So a gallon holds more than a litre, nearly 4 litres.
items.answer: More. A gallon holds a little less than 4 litres.
items.question: The chart gives 1 gallon as about 3.79 L. Does a gallon hold more or less than a litre?
items.checkpoint: Read the chart's rounded number to tell which unit is bigger.
items.misconception: Taking the smaller unit to be the gallon because the word is unfamiliar, without reading the chart card.

steps: The chart gives 1 foot as about 0.305 m.
So the plank is about 0.915 m long.
Adding the chart number three times needs no decimal to be multiplied.
items.question: A plank is about 3 feet long. About how many metres is that?
items.checkpoint: For a few lots of a unit, add the chart number that many times.
items.misconception: Adding the 3 to the chart number once, instead of adding the chart number three times.

steps: The chart gives 1 kg as about 2.2 pounds.
The chart's numbers are rounded, so every answer made from them is about, not exact.
items.answer: About 6.6 pounds. The chart's numbers are rounded, so the answer is close, not exact.
items.question: A parcel weighs about 3 kg. About how many pounds is that, and why is the answer only about?
items.checkpoint: Every answer made from the chart is about, not exact, because its numbers are rounded.
items.misconception: Saying the parcel is exactly 6.6 pounds, when the chart's 2.2 is itself rounded.

learn.shape: Worked items, shown solved, mandatory before practice unlocks.
learn.selection: Fixed order, walking the phases from the first to the last.
learn.content_criterion: One per phase, so Learn walks the whole topic and stops.

items.question: Name one unit of weight on the chart that is not a metric unit.
Which of these measures capacity: a mile, a gallon or an ounce?
Is an inch longer or shorter than a centimetre?
items.final_answer: Longer: the chart gives 1 inch as about 2.54 cm

items.question: The chart gives 1 yard as about 0.914 m. Is a yard longer or shorter than a metre?
items.final_answer: Shorter, a little less than 1 m

items.question: A book is about 2 inches thick. About how many centimetres is that?
A walk is about 2 miles long. About how many kilometres is that?
A pot holds about 3 gallons. About how many litres is that, and why do we say about?
items.final_answer: About 11.37 L, because 3.79 + 3.79 + 3.79 = 11.37, and the chart's numbers are rounded

items.question: A letter weighs about 2 ounces. About how many grams is that, and is the answer exact?
items.final_answer: About 56.7 g, because 28.35 + 28.35 = 56.7. It is not exact, because the chart's numbers are rounded

teaching_notes: Say about with every answer made from the chart: its numbers are rounded. Where a question needs a few lots of a chart number, add them rather than multiply a decimal, which has not been taught. Compare sizes before any number: a mile is a little longer than one and a half kilometres, and a kilogram is a little more than two pounds. Leave out the chart's line from centimetres to feet, which is cut short.

On the first phase unit cards are dragged into bins for length, weight and capacity. On the second a tapped card lays two bars side by side, roughly to scale. On the third a Stack button lays copies of one card end to end and the child adds their metric numbers. On the fourth an About stamp is pressed onto the answer before it turns green. The given measure is deep blue and the card in use amber. No decimal is multiplied or divided anywhere. Pointer events only, no assets, no network. Build it from the writeup and the tool build spec, not from this paragraph (maths_agent/TOOL_BUILD_SPEC.md). Each phase comes from writeup.phases, with its screen, action, reward and spoken line; its tries field is the hint ladder and its wrong list is what the stage does about a wrong answer, redrawn in steps on the working area with nothing marked and nothing reset. The one surprise is writeup.delight. The look and the sounds come from tool_config.style, voice and audio.
